content.en: The un-lockdown is under way, and some privileged ones like us sit in our homes working and watching and reading day after day about the endless cruelty that is being heaped all around us. On migrant workers who walked miles and miles in their desperation to return home, on informal sector workers who have not had a decent meal to eat, and nowhere to call home. While we sink further into our misery, our thoughts move back and forth on all that has transpired in the last many months: what happened to all the anti CAA-NRC-NPR protestors hounded and threatened, their protest sites ripped apart? What happened to the victims of the violence that erupted in North East Delhi, largely Muslims, many of whom find themselves being arrested and jailed for the very violence that destroyed their lives? What new forms will the peaceful protests against the unjust CAA-NRC-NPR look like? In fact, will we ever see them take over the streets again? Do the whitewashed walls of Shaheen Bagh still hold our collective rage, and the imagination of our democratic nation? At times like these, looking back and reminiscing seems like an almost indecent luxury. Nevertheless, reflect and write we must, for the raging powerful light of Shaheen Baghs have shown us the way for eons to come.
The light begins to change.

en: I am a Miya, My serial number in the NRC is 200543
Next summer. Will you hate him, as you hate me?

content.en: - Hafiz Ahmed, Miya poet, Assam
It was in August 2019, when the figure of ‘1.9 million people’ in Assam hit the headlines

popover.text: Final Assam NRC list released, excludes over 19 lakh applicants.

content.en: . Who are these people and what will happen to them was a question that stuck like a fishbone in the throat of the nation. The Supreme Court mandated and monitored exercise culminated in the publication of the National Register of Citizens
(NRC)

in Assam, and a ‘mere’ 6% of 33 million people who had applied to establish their belonging, were deemed ‘illegal immigrants’. Never mind if you and your family lived in Assam for decades, even from pre-independence times. Just suck it up if you are on the list and the rest of your family not, so what if one odd sibling is not included. Shut-up. Just shut-up with your ranting and your prayers, if you were not organised and resourceful enough to have had your papers in order. And if you are who you say you are, especially a Hindu a ‘genuine Indian citizen’, who god-forbid-how, found yourself excluded, then the government will do many a somersault to challenge the NRC Coordinator, the process and the list, and attempt to use the CAA in order to bring you back into the fold

popover.text: Speculation had been rife that out of the 19 lakh people excluded from the NRC in Assam, as many as 14 lakh were Hindus.

content.en: . But if you are on the ‘wrong side’ of the current prevailing idea of community/religion/ethnicity, then buckle up to make your case to the Foreigners Tribunal, or risk being packed off to a detention centre

image.credit: Political graffiti near Jamia Millia Islamia University, Delhi

content.en: While talk of the NRC project had been on since 2015, this development in Assam was a test balloon to check the temperature, to increase the heat. How much is too much? After all, the abrogation of Article 370 in Kashmir had just been carried out, and the applause of how smooth an operation it was could be heard all the way from the stage of ‘Howdy, Modi!’ to the staged sights of foreign diplomats in the idyllic settings of the Dal lake

popover.text: Second batch of foreign envoys enjoy Shikara ride on Dal Lake.

content.en: . Then, not much was said of the criminalization of Muslim men with the passage of the Triple Talaq Bill, right?! And the judgment on the Babri Masjid-Ram Janmabhoomi dispute, just forget about it. Don’t you know it’s now legally established that the land does not belong to ‘you’, it belongs to those, who, even the judgment says, wrongfully demolished it. Just get on with the programme.
Darkness descends.

The least we can say about the BJP is that it’s a party which keeps its promises. One such promise made in its election manifesto was to bring about a ‘Citizenship Amendment Bill 2016’ (CAB). Soon after the BJP led government’s victory in the 2019 General Elections, the noise around the CAB grew much louder and as did the one for a nationwide NRC. Of course, the purported reason for the CAB was to fast-track citizenship for persecuted Hindus, Jains, Sikhs, Buddhists, Christians and Parsis from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan. All ‘others’, especially Muslims, can wait their turn to be thrown out, if declared non-citizens. And others like trans* persons, adivasis, and countless others without adequate documents or any other way to prove their belonging, can wait and watch from the sidelines. Not to forget, that all this talk of protecting persecuted minorities came in the back drop of the Indian government deporting the persecuted Rohingya Muslims to Myanmar

popover.text: 22 Myanmar nationals including Rohingya deported since August 2017.

content.en: “Pakistan’s Hindu community unanimously rejects this bill, which is tantamount to dividing India on communal lines,” said the Pakistan Hindu Council.

“We, the Christians of Pakistan, are not at all interested [in taking] refuge in India... Modi’s citizenship bill does not favour the minorities at all as it is discriminatory and against basic human rights.”

popover.text: Hindus of Pakistan reject CAA, do not want Indian Prime Minister Modi’s offer of citizenship.

content.en: “There are genuine concerns and apprehensions in Bangladesh that the NRC and CAA might unleash an exodus of Bengali-speaking people from Assam and Muslims attempting to escape persecution in India. After having taken in nearly a million Rohingya refugees fleeing persecution in Myanmar, Bangladesh cannot take in any more.”

popover.text: How India’s CAA, NRC affect Bangladesh.

content.en: In October 2019, when the country was in the grip of Dussehra-Diwali-Durgapuja-Amazon-Great-Diwali-Sale fever, and the fate of those 1.9 million was still unknown, Home Minister Amit Shah announced that the National Register of Citizens will be implemented in the entire country

popover.text: NRC to be implemented in whole country.

content.en: . Just days before this announcement, setting the stage, the Home Minister, speaking at an event celebrating the 26th foundation day of the National Human Rights Commission, had urged India, and the world, to view human rights violations in India with the ‘Indian outlook’. Further adding that, ‘under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership, India is moving towards a scenario where there will be no human rights violations!’ (well, what to say about the NHRC

popover.text: India’s National Human Rights Commission is defeating its own purpose.

content.en: ). Concurrently, the government was also making steady headway in fulfilling its electoral promise of bringing about the Citizenship Amendment Bill.

But the government had a problem on their hands – the 1.9 million who fell out of the NRC web in Assam weren’t all muslims, who the intention had been to comb out. So during the winter session of the Parliament, amidst hue and cry from across the country, the Citizenship Amendment Act on 11 December 2019. The CAB was now CAA
and the NRC was being discussed alongside the NPR. The National Population Register (NPR

) is a ‘Register of usual residents of the country. The last National Population Register was collected in 2010 along with the house listing phase of Census of India 2011’, says the MHA website. These developments caused an incredible amount of confusion, panic and insecurity especially for the muslim minority in the country. How to prove one’s citizenry!

popover.text: Can you prove you are an Indian citizen? Take the Assam NRC test.

content.en: As people began scrambling for birth certificates and other documents, many also began to question thegovernment, asking that it stop speaking in forked tongues. The ‘NRC will definitely be implemented all over thecountry, we are ready to roll it out at a cost of about Rs. 30,000 crores,’ said one tongue; while the other said,‘you have nothing to fear, NRC isn’t here!’

popover.text: Why PM Modi chose to contradict Amit Shah’s NRC vow.

content.en: Frustrated at the stupid subjects asking stupid questions, the Home Minister finally said ‘Aap chronology samajhiye’, and you know, that’s exactly what we, the people, did.
Things get darker.

Soon after CAA 2019 became the law of the land, many protests, dharnas, rallies, press conferences sprung up all over the country, and by the signs of it, the government wasn’t in a mood for any of that. After all, good, abiding citizens are just meant to buy (with our duly demonetised currency) every half-truth and full lie sold to us through parliamentary statements, sarkari slogans, ads, the godi media and every other weapon in the propaganda arsenal. But, the people, it seems, hadn’t got the script.

Not just in the ‘legally designated’ protest spaces like Jantar Mantar in Delhi, Azad Maidan in Bombay, Vidhan Soudha in Bangalore, but also in college campuses, residential areas, on streets and in marketplaces, across the country, voices against CAA-NRC-NPR started getting louder. Uff, what a nuisance the subjects are being! Time to crack down on, and stem the tide. And what better place to start than at a fairly routine protest within the campus of the Jamia Millia Islamia (JMI) University in Delhi.

Uninvited into the campus, the Delhi Police threw stones at the protestors inside the campus and then broke down the main gate, lathi charged the students, barged into the library and smashed furniture, light fixtures, and of course, student’s bodies, busting into women’s toilets to drag female students out by their hair, and oh yes, let’s not forget, threw firebombs into buses and then claimed they were just trying to quell the violence. (Phew! Just catching our breath). If you haven’t still seen the video,
here it is.

Maybe we should send it to the NHRC who’s recent ‘findings’ on the events echoes the voice of the central government and the Delhi Police, and says, ‘the students did it!’ At about the same time, the students of Aligarh Muslim University were holding a peaceful protest against the CAA. Again, the security forces indulged in lathi charge, firing of tear gas shells and rubber pellets at the protesting students for no valid reason on December 15, 2019. Someone see a pattern here?

image.credit: Jury makes the final presentation at The Peoples' Tribunal

content.en: Peoples’ Tribunal on Contested Citizenship, Assam
Just days after the final National Register of Citizens (NRC) was published in Assam, a people’s tribunal was organised in New Delhi to discuss issues related to citizenship, titled,
People’s Tribunal on Contested Citizenship in Assam – Constitutional Processes and the Human Cost.

Hearing the testimonies of those excluded from the final list of NRC and various leading experts, the jury comprising former SC judges Madan B Lokur and Kurian Joseph, former Delhi High Court Chief Justice AP Shah and Professor Faizan Mustafa, Vice Chancellor, Nalsar University of Law, Hyderabad, former Planning Commission member Syeda Hamid, Ambassador Deb Mukherjee, Githa Hariharan of Indian Writers’ Forum and Professor Monirul Hussain, said, ‘We all agree that the NRC has spawned a humanitarian crisis. We worry because there are no signs of this crisis abating. Large numbers of minorities in Assam, whether religious, linguistic or ethnic, have lived with the fear of being told that they don’t belong in this country. They may, at any time, be marked doubtful voters (or D-Voter) and prevented from exercising their franchise. A local border police constable can, again, at any time, accuse them of being foreigners and refer their cases to a detention centre. Even after the final register, there are many demands for selective reverification.’
Thanks for the interruption!
Winds of change start wafting in from near the Yamuna.

Anyway, the parents of the young students who got thrashed did what parents and in fact, any decent people would do. Stepped out and said, ‘stop it! enough is enough’. Of course, the JMIs, JNUs, and other students groups, civil/democratic/women’s rights and other liberals did it, but it was a working class neighbourhood called Shaheen Bagh that stands along the banks of the Yamuna and on the Magenta line of the Delhi Metro, really ‘did it’. Hundreds of women, with their children tucked under the armpit, got out of their homes, and blocked the street in protest. We all know these women, they are same burqas clad women who the government had to ‘rescue’ by criminalising their triple-talaq-giving-husbands

popover.text: Historical wrong done to Muslim women corrected: PM Modi on Triple Talaq Bill.

content.en: . Newsflash! They have a voice, an opinion, and an imagination. And amazingly, the capacity to change the course of history and protests in the country, irrespective of what has followed since.

The women of Shaheen Bagh, the dadis of Shaheen Bagh, the children of Shaheen Bagh occupied the main Kalindi Kunj road and started a peaceful sit-in with only one demand: ‘Take back CAA-NRC-NPR’. And soon, Shaheen Baghs were springing up all over the city – in Khureji Khas, Jama Masjid, Turkman Gate, Shahi Eidgah, Nizamuddin, Seelampur, Hauz Rani, Chand Bagh, Inderlok... 27 plus sites. And beyond Delhi there sprung, literally, hundreds of protests sites across Lucknow, Kolkata, Ranchi, Gaya, Kanpur, Hyderabad, Patna, Bangalore, Kolkata, Varanasi... in Europe, the US, Canada and so on.

As day became night, and nights blossomed into songs, slogans and chatter, these sites attracted to themselves many like us, battered and weary in our quest for ‘woh subah kabhi toh aayegi’. Spending whatever time we could with the women and students, soaking in the energy and doing our bit: talking to the women, volunteering at the medical counter, discovering new slogans, singing and performing, teaching and playing with the children at the Savitribai Phule and other libraries/ activity centres set up for the children at many of the sites, raising issues related to the CAA, religious and caste discrimination, the idea of the nation and much more.

The idea of the Shaheen Baghs was like an eternal spring – a fresh, sparkling source of untiring energy for a community which has been targeted by lynchings, harassment and systematic political exclusion over the past several years, and whose defence mechanism has largely been to invisibilize itself in public. But let’s be honest, they were much more than the voice of the community, they were the voice we all had been seeking in our so-called ‘intersectional politics.’ Young and old women, many of them illiterate, who were soon effortlessly drawing their strength and articulation from, and teaching us a lesson or two about, the Constitution, Babasaheb Ambedkar, Fatima Sheikh, Savitribai Phule, Bhagat Singh, Ashfaqulla Khan, Ram Prasad Bismil, and Gandhi. After a very, very long time of hate, divisive and destructive politics, we saw a glimmer of democracy re-imagined, citizenship owned and asserted in ways so creative that they will forever be etched in our minds. As we stood/sat together reading the Preamble in multiple languages at India Gate, with Radhika Vemula and Saira Bano on Republic Day, singing the national anthem on New Year’s Eve with a sense of belief in its possibilities! What a miracle that was/is.

image.credit: New Year's Eve at the Shaheen Bagh protest site

content.en: An image, an idea, that we have not seen evoked in movements since possibly the independence struggle, was the use of the Tricolour. The Flag was everywhere, held high. The National Anthem was sung daily at many sit-ins. As reading the Preamble became the norm at protests across the country, we the people, who believe, that we don’t need to wear our patriotism on our sleeve pivoted between cringing at this overt show of nationalism, and the awe we felt for those who reclaimed these symbols from the clutches of the right wing. Putting an end to any questions about their ‘Indian-ness’, perhaps. Making us think about our politics and privileges in completely new ways.

Simultaneously, there were multiple protest events across the country. If so many hundreds of thousands marched to Azad Maidan in Mumbai, that the only way to see the whole crowd was from the top of a multi- storeyed building; coordinated national marches led by women, trans* and queer communities, students etc; and so many plays and skits and songs and verses and memes and online action... that all spoke to resisting the CAA-NRC-NPR package deal that is being thrust upon us. #Reject CAA #RejectNRC #Reject NPR

As the popularity of these protests grew, the international attention began to be a problem for the State and its fellows. The government (both Delhi and Central) refused to meet the protestors and engage with their demands, despite the most loving missives from the protestors. Instead, right wing groups repeatedly attempted to ‘ukhaad nikaalo’ the protests, the state arbitrarily withdrew permissions given for protests, blocked metro stations to prevent people from reaching rally and protest sites, picked people up from the sites and took them on a Dilli-darshan for hours to try to stop them from protesting. Of course, we the (problematic) citizens would turn around and rejoin the protesting masses the moment they let us off in some obscure corner of the city. And thank heavens we did, because those were days we could still protest on the streets, remember?

But let’s face it, all the romance of the protests aside, things were getting a bit crazy. Take for example the trajectory of cases against these two 19 year olds: Ram Bhagat Gopal Sharma, shot at the protestors at JMI screaming ‘ye lo azaadi’, while the police stood around with folded arms and let a student get injured. Amulya Leona went onto the stage of an anti-CAA event in Bangalore organised by the All India Majlis-e-Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen (AIMIM ), and proclaimed ‘Long Live All Nations’... and among the nations she said ‘zindabad’ to was Pakistan. She was charged with sedition under the dreaded UAPA, while Sharma was out on bail within the week or so. Leona finally received bail only after spending 6 months in jail. Meanwhile, someone threw a petrol bomb at the protest site in Shaheen Bagh, the police did an unprovoked lathi charge at the Hauz Rani site, the story was turning...

In the midst of it, came the Delhi elections, marked by just one thing: talk of governance by the AAP party, and hate speech against the Muslim community by the BJP and its allies. Deeply shocked by this, Saheli, along with 175 other feminist and human rights organisations and activists, issued an Open Letter to the Prime Minister on 3 February 2020, saying, ‘Vote for BJP or you will get raped? Is this your message to Delhi’s women? Your party is also exhorting mobs to aim bullets at women & children... Fight the election upholding the dignity of our Constitution.’

content.credit: Protest site at Shahi Eidgah, Delhi

content.en: It's a night without end.

It was February 2020, but it was reminiscent of 1984 Delhi and 2002 Gujarat, when many of us watched as horrific visuals unfolded on our television screens. Smoky skies and armed mobs running amok burning houses, shops, hurtling bricks as violence erupted in North East Delhi on 23 February, and continued for another few days. While NE Delhi was burning, a few kilometres away the President of the United States of America, Donald Trump was enjoying a lavish banquet hosted by the State.

popover.text: From aloo tikki to malpua: Trump attends lavish banquet hosted by President Kovind.

content.en: It was ‘Namaste Trump’ time, after all.

In the next few days, as more details emerged and bodies were found rotting in the drains of NE Delhi, the gravity of what had happened began to sink in. Of the 53 who lost their lives, two-thirds belonged to the Muslim community. As stories of mosques (14, according to one estimate

popover.text: Fourteen Delhi mosques and a dargah that were burnt by Hindutva vigilantes in three days.

content.en: ) being set on fire, and the destruction of mainly Muslim owned businesses and properties started pouring in, it became clear that this was communally motivated. Several areas of NE Delhi were also sites of the anti-CAA women protests, and many believed that the peaceful protesters would not move until their one and only demand was met. Was this planned attacked a way of silencing them? Perhaps BJP’s Kapil Mishra, of the ‘desh ke gaddaron ko, goli maaro saalon ko’ fame, can throw some light on this

popover.text: BJP’s ‘Goli Maro’ Candidate Kapil Mishra Loses From Delhi’s Model Town.

content.en: ? If you are an optimist, you may also ask, what was the police doing

popover.text: Actions of cops during NE Delhi riots to be assessed.

content.en: ? According to many accounts, the police was present often as spectators to the violence around them. There are also accounts that claim that they actively participated. It seemed that they only moved into the area in large numbers a few days later, and that too after the Delhi High Court ordered them to assist move the injured to hospitals

popover.text: HC Judge Who Pulled Up Delhi Police Over Riots Shunted Out by Modi Govt.

content.en: . The hospitals were no better.

A report titled, “The Role of Health Systems in Responding to Communal Violence” by the Jan Swasthya Abhiyan (JSA), speaks of the apathy with which victims of violence were treated at government hospitals, that is, if they managed to reach one because mobs continued to obstruct the movement of ambulances. At the hospitals themselves, there were several instances of patients not bring provided with adequate treatment, with one doctor even calling the victim a terrorist and extremist, and cruelly, bodies not being handed over to families for days on end.

In a letter to Delhi CM Kejriwal, the JSA elaborated, “We have also been made aware of instances where hospitals are denying admission to injured persons whose MLCs were done in a different hospital, without the MLC number and treatment records. Families and patients are thus being penalized and harassed for not producing documents which are being denied to them in the first place... Hospitals are not proactively supporting families of injured people... families are running from pillar to post to identify their missing relatives. Multiple individuals who have been victims of violence have reported instances of being subjected to discriminatory language by staff members at hospitals. A few people have even expressed fear of going to government hospitals, instead choosing to access critical care at local clinics.”
Meanwhile, the state, was spinning great tales of conspiracy aimed at shifting the blame on to the victims for the violence

popover.text: Rescripting north-east Delhi riots – and the question of justice.

content.en: – a script being clearly followed in the spate of arrests of student and other activists from the anti CAA movement as being masterminds of a leftist- jihadi-radical (will someone please explain what kind of politics this is?) conspiracy

popover.text: Delhi Riots 2020: A Critique of Two Purported Fact-Finding Reports.

content.en: In the weeks that followed, Eidgah-Mustafabad became a relief camp site where about 1200 people took shelter, people whose homes were burnt, livelihood destroyed, and those who were too fearful of going back. The camp, of course, had no proper tenting, no toilets and nothing for people to eat. Add to that the relentless rains that lashed Delhi those days, soaking the mattresses and robbing victims of even their sleep.

Several citizen initiatives sprang up in response to these terrible events: to offer rescue and refuge to victims; to offer medical aid and relief support; to remind government officials, agencies, bodies of their constitutional duty to protect all citizens; to reach out with food, clothing, sanitary products, rations and other essentials; to counsel and help the old and the young and the children in this time of trauma; to offer immediate aid to those disabled or paralyzed due to injuries. Peace committees were formed to reach out to at the neighbourhood level. Called ‘Aman ki Aawazein’, we went from one locality to another with messages of peace, justice, harmony and togetherness. A meal here, a song there, a poem read, a sharing of information of rights guaranteed by the courts... all sharing a moment in solidarity in times of duress.
Excerpts from the first citizen’s report titled, ‘Let us heal our Dilli’
by Farah Naqvi, Sarojini N, Navsharan Singh, Naveen Chander.

‘The targeting of Muslims in North east Delhi reminded one distinctly of the targeting of Sikhs in Delhi in 1984 and of Muslims in Gujarat 2002. The targeted damage to property and means of livelihood for people who live on the edge of survival is truly vile. Thelas burnt, small shops burnt, autorickshaws burnt, e-rickshaws burnt, a scrap market burnt. These are means of livelihood for some of India’s poorest people.’

‘In one case that we encountered, the attack on Hindu properties was by right-wing mobs themselves. An autorickshaw owner/driver, on the main road outside Gokulpuri flailed helplessly but angrily at the injustice of what happened to him – two of his autorickshaws which he proudly pointed out say ‘Jai Mata Di’ on the back, were burnt because in one of them he was ferrying Muslim passengers and the mob probably thought he was Muslim too. “I am a Hindu!” he kept saying.’

‘In Mustafabad people were angry and said the central government was busy with the Trump visit instead of ensuring early deployment of army or police, which would have saved lives and protected their properties. Even after the attack, no one from the state or central government has reached out to victims. And it has been nearly 4 days now, to the first attack on Sunday (Feb 23). There was NO relief effort. No food, no places for the displaced to stay, no one to call. At Chand Bagh, we were asked if we could arrange food for 200 families of labourers being accommodated in a masjid.’ Complete report
here.

Even as the Covid-19 crisis became a global pandemic, the central government refused to take back its order to start updation of the NPR along with house listing for the Census 2021 from 1 April, 2020. So more than 1000 women from across 20 states of India, wrote to every state Chief Minister in the country saying, “NPR presents a clear danger to women, so we demand de-linking of NPR from census house listing.” Addressing a crowded press conference in Delhi, women rights activists, including Annie Raja, Farah Naqvi, Anjali Bhardwaj, Vani Subramanian, Meera Sanghamitra, Mariam Dhawle and Poonam Kaushik said, “Women constitute nearly 50% of India’s population, and all women, irrespective of caste and religious community will be affected by this regime that puts our citizenship to test in a totally arbitrary and frightening manner.” At the same time, the activists welcomes the fact that Kerala and West bengal had already issued stay orders on the roll out of the NPR.

And what was the central government doing meanwhile? Within days of Lockdown 1.0 the relief camp was shut and people were left to fend for themselves. All the protest sites, including Shaheen Bagh, were removed, and the vibrant anti CAA-NRC-NPR graffiti white washed (literally)

popover.text: Police Remove Jamia Graffiti, Twitter Reminds Them of ‘Priorities’.

content.en: . But that’s all they can do... kyunki ‘hum dekhenge’ (Faiz must be pleased

popover.text: Dissenting with Faiz: How ‘Hum Dekhenge’ has been adapted in protests across India.

content.en: ), and also because ‘hum kaagaz nahi dikhayenge’ by Varun Grover, the two popular anthems of this movement. The peaceful protests ended, many of us argued that given the situation it was perhaps wise to do so. However, what stays alive is the vision that imagines this country as one belonging to everyone.

The Covid-19 health crisis has rapidly become an economic crisis, an employment crisis and a migrant crisis – exposing all faultlines and fissures. No amount of thali clanging, diya lighting, made-up economic packages will undo what has been witnessed, what is being lived through. But even at this time, the anti-Muslim sentiment runs deep as was illustrated by calls to boycott Muslim-owned businesses

popover.text: Covid an excuse to push Indian Muslims out of informal sector jobs.

content.en: , and the targeting of the members of the Tablighi Jamaat who were held responsible for the pandemic because of an international summit they held in early March. The nation communalized a virus

. As our focus shifted to providing relief to, too many to count, Covid-19 impacted communities: daily wagers, victims of violence in NE Delhi, migrants on the move, sex workers, trans* persons and so on, the State’s focus shifted to targeting anti-CAA protestors. (Joint statement by feminists follows.).

Maybe, this time, the light will break through. What happens next? Who knows. But it seems that the chasm between the haves, the ones who belong, whose citizenry is guaranteed; and all the rest, has become a painful putrid gash. This hurt was for all to see in the plight of migrant workers during lockdown. Thrown out of work, walking endlessly on foot, dying of hunger, dragging along their measly belongings and their broken hearts.

A lot is to be said about what the government did and didn’t during this crisis, but that’s a piece for another time. The SC intervened only in early June providing some relief, however belated, to the migrant workers

popover.text: SC gives centre, states 15 days to send migrant workers back home.

content.en: . But can we unsee the gut wrenching video of that dead migrant and her child on a train platform in Bihar, the incident in Aurangabad where exhausted workers, sleeping on a train track were crushed to death

popover.text: How can we stop this if they sleep on tracks, SC says on migrants killed in Aurangabad, rejects shelter plea.

content.en: . There are too many to count...

Betrayed by the glittering cities, by the courts and the governments. Maybe the migrant workers will never come back to polish and shine our lives, to make our cars, serve us at restaurants, to wait endlessly at labour chowks for our largesse, to care for our children ‘just like their own’... or maybe the companies who didn’t have the resources to give them their salaries at a time of crisis will suddenly find the funds to charter planes to get them back!

image.credit: A Saheli set of stickers against the Citizen’s Amendment Bill, and the increasing ways in which the State seeks to monitor, and put our lives under surveillance, but refuses to treat certain sections of the people as citizens.

3 May, 2020: We, the undersigned, strongly condemn the brazenly malicious attacks, arrests and intimidation by the Delhi Police of Muslim women, students and activists, as well as other citizens who have spoken up against the unconstitutional moves of the present ruling dispensation. Media reports that about 800 + anti-CAA protesters have been detained or arrested since the Covid 19 lockdown, which means they have had little or no access to lawyers and legal aid, and their families given no information of their whereabouts for extended periods after they were in custody. The impunity with which the Delhi Police is carrying out this sweep under direct orders from the Home Ministry is facilitated by the reduced media, public and legal scrutiny under the lockdown. As feminists, we decry this systematic crackdown on, and mis-representation of, the peaceful and constitutional anti-CAA-NRC-NPR movement. Led so powerfully by Muslim women across the country, these protests witnessed a new wave of women stepping out in their own neighbourhoods in huge numbers, defying social structures and asserting their rights as citizens of a secular, democratic republic—one of the most historic moments and movements, since independence. In Delhi itself, from the Dadis of Shaheen Bagh to the spirited women from Jamia, Hauz Rani, Jama Masjid, Nizamuddin, Seelampur, etc, the women’s spectacular leadership and the solidarities they formed across communities and locations inspired millions across the world, but evidently, also shook the foundations of the ruling elite. After all, until these women organised themselves with such clarity, and commitment to democratic values, the only use the government had for them was as symbols of repression to be ‘saved’ from Muslim customary practices such as the Triple Talaq.

GULFISHA, 25, is one such young muslim woman who emerged a leader in the Seelampur anti-CAA protest. An MBA student, Gulfisha has reportedly been arrested by the police on 9th April, but until this day, the details remain blurry. She has been languishing in judicial custody under false charges of sedition, without proper access to her family or lawyer. The Covid lockdown has brought jail mulakats to a standstill, and no alternative means of communication such as telephonic contact are available to be apprised of her state of health or well-being. The same holds for numerous men from Seelampur who were allegedly picked up by the police at about the same time as Gulfisha, although their exact whereabouts are not known. SAFOORA ZARGAR, 30, member of the Jamia Coordination Committee has been arrested despite being three months’ pregnant—at a time when overcrowding in prisons and have become a huge concern worldwide. Former Municipal Councillor, ISHRAT JAHAN, active in the Khureji protest has been in jail for over a month now, and been subjected to custodial torture. Her co-accused, Khalid Saifi emerged from police custody with both his legs as well as two fingers broken—indicating brutal torture. We have good reason to fear for the rights and safety of Gulfisha, Safoora, Ishrat and others like them: as women, as undertrial prisoners, and as those falsely charged under the draconian Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA).

Some of the other student activists arrested and slapped with draconian charges and sent to judicial custody include Meeran Haider (President, RJD Youth Wing, Delhi), Sharjeel Imam (JNU scholar), Shifa-Ur-Rehman (President, Jamia Alumni Association). Dr. Umar Khalid of United Against Hate has also been reportedly slapped with UAPA and is ‘under investigation’. In an unprecedented and shameless move, the Delhi Police has now even booked Zafarul Islam Khan, Chairman, Delhi Minorities Commission under sedition charges! We must remember that inspired by Shaheen Bagh, sit-in protests led by Muslim women were held in 200+ locations across the country. Holding up images of Savitri Bai, Fatima Sheikh, Babasaheb Ambedkar, painting protest graffiti and reading the Preamble, reciting poetry and slogans upholding constitutional values and communal harmony, this was a tremendously powerful assertion of rights and resistance, of historically marginalized women creating the possibility of a new nation of emancipation, justice, equality and dignity. In response, the majoritarian forces of the Hindu right, shifted the register of contestation by unleashing multiple attacks on these gatherings, culminating in a pre-planned communal pogrom targeting the Muslims in North-East Delhi.

The government, unwilling to dialogue with the women, chose the masculinist response of trying to crush them. Its message is clear—those who dare challenge its fascist, patriarchal, communal, classist and casteist nature will be meted the harshest State sanctions. Countless detentions, interrogation and intimidation of women and student activists from many anti-CAA protest sites and universities like Jamia, bear testimony to how brazenly the State is using everything, including the pandemic, to silence more than just one Gulfisha or Safoora; to warn all Muslim women who dare to speak out. For minority communities to exist in India today seems to be a provocation, for them to question and think seems to be a greater trouble, and of course, to protest and sing songs of azaadi is apparently just too much.

Not surprisingly, a malicious and false narrative that ‘the peaceful protests by women were the cause of the violence in Delhi’ has been propagated by the police, fanned by sections of the media and vested interests to camouflage the explicit political nature of the violence, carried out with the collusion and participation of security forces. Despite claims by the police of ‘finding the real culprits’, the organized and premeditated nature of the violence on the minority community and the great asymmetry in losses and deaths between affected communities is yet to be accounted for. Right-wing leaders of the BJP such as Kapil Mishra and Anurag Thakur who openly threatened violence have not even been named in FIRs. Those who fired at gatherings are out on bail. Reports of ‘out-of-towners’ brought in to perpetuate the violence have yet to be subjects of investigation.

After all of this, the community which bore the brunt of the communal violence most, including the peaceful women protesters and men, is being projected as the ‘aggressor’ and demeaned in numerous ways through vicious propaganda. Hundreds of Muslims are being picked up and incarcerated. There is no clarity on the total number of FIRs, arrests and detentions. Muslim women and other activists who worked with them in solidarity towards a shared concept of citizenship and feminist sisterhood are also being systematically vilified. Media reports that in the last some days, the police has seized the phones of AISA activist Kawalpreet Kaur and few activists of Pinjra Tod. Worrying accounts of women students who were active in the peaceful protests, being targeted are also coming to the fore. Taking cognizance of such ground realities, the Delhi High Court as recently as on 27th April, directed the Delhi Police to comply with the DK Basu guidelines regarding arrests and detentions.

In the long run, these attacks by the State will affect far more than members of just one community. Much like the NRC project that is bound to deprive the poor and marginalized across religious groups of citizenship rights, the present focus on terrorizing Muslims instead of tackling the Covid-19 pandemic reveals a deep apathy towards safeguarding the lives and well-being of millions of toiling poor across the country, many of whom belong to the ‘majority’ community.

We remember with hope and inspiration the vibrant anti-CAA protests across the country from December to February. We remember that while the State was firing tear gas shells in libraries and mercilessly lathi-charging peaceful protesters and students, while the police stood by as vigilante gunmen opened fire, these protesters stood strong and fearless in their determination against the Hindutva project. They are the conscience keepers of the nation, and we salute them! The actions of the State only reveal how much it fears such voices, and how far it will go to subvert the cause of truth and justice. We declare our unflinching solidarity with the Muslim women, students and activists who worked together as harbingers of peace and shall defeat sinister attempts to project them in bad light by the state and vested interests.
We demand:

en.text: Delhi Police must immediately make public all FIRs, arrests and detentions with their legal status and conduct a free and fair investigation into all the incidents of violence.
False cases against peaceful anti-CAA protesters must be dropped, and all those arrested on trumped-up charges must be released immediately.
Real culprits of the violence in Delhi must be booked, including the likes of Kapil Mishra, Anurag Thakur, Parvesh Verma and others who instigated hate, sparked and perpetuated the violence.
Detentions, intimidation & harassment of those who assert the democratic right to protest must stop.
Prisons must be de-congested as per orders of the Apex Court and all political prisoners released.
UAPA and the Sedition law must be repealed.
